docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The purpose of this individual block diagram is to showcse the hardware architecture, electrical interfaces, and signal flow for the Servo Motor Subsystem of Team's Modular Spider Leg.

Key system parameters: * Power Source & Levels: The board is powered by an external 9V DC wall adapter, which is stepped down via a linear regulator (LM7805) to a regulated 5V DC supply. This 5V domain powers the servo motor and the microcontroller. * Actuator & Sensors: The primary actuator is a standard servo motor (e.g., TowerPro SG90) driven by a 5V PWM signal directly from the microcontroller. * Team Connections: Operating as a "spoke" in our team's hub-and-spoke method, this board connects to the main hub board using the standard 8-pin ribbon connector. * Signal Flow: The central hub sends digital position commands via a serial connection on Pin 1 to the PIC18F57Q43 microcontroller's UART RX pin. The microcontroller translates this command and outputs a digital parallel PWM signal to drive the servo motor to the target angle.

docs.title: Driver Nano 1 (Servo + Display)
docs.text:
This page covers the components for Driver Nano 1: the hip-joint servo and the diagnostic display. Driver Nano 1 receives target positions from the Main Processor Nano over the command/feedback bus (I2C), drives the hip joint, shows leg status on the display, and reports status back.

Selection criteria used for both components

  • Runs from the 5 V logic domain used by the Nano, with as few extra supply rails as possible.
  • Has a manufacturer or distributor datasheet (required by the course).
  • Uses few Nano pins and little RAM (ATmega328P: 2 KB SRAM, 32 KB flash).
  • Does not use the Nano's hardware I2C pins (A4/A5), which are reserved for the command bus to the Main Nano.
  • Hip joint torque requirement: TODO: required torque = m × g × L × 2 (safety factor), where m = leg mass beyond the hip, L = distance from the hip axis to the center of mass. Insert your numbers here.

Hip Joint Servo (Rotary Actuator)

  1. Hitec HS-485HB standard analog servo

    • $28.99/each
    • HS-485HB product page at ServoCity
    • HS-485HB manufacturer datasheet
    Pros Cons Position control is built in: the internal potentiometer and amplifier hold the commanded angle, so the Nano only outputs one 50 Hz PWM signal (Servo library, any digital pin) and no driver IC is needed. Stall current is 1.0 A at 4.8 V and 1.2 A at 6 V per the datasheet, so the regulator and wiring must be sized for it, and the servo cannot be powered from the Nano's 5V pin or USB. Stall torque of 4.8 kgf·cm at 4.8 V and 6.0 kgf·cm at 6 V in a 45 g package gives the highest torque per gram of the three options. Karbonite (plastic) gears can strip under shock loads such as a leg strike, and metal-gear servos cost more. Runs from the same 4.8–6 V range as the logic, so no second, higher-voltage supply is needed. The servo gives no position output, so the Nano cannot confirm that the joint reached the angle. The status sent to the Main Nano is the commanded value, not a measured one. The datasheet lists stall current, idle current (8–10 mA), speed (0.22 s/60° at 4.8 V), deadband, and dimensions, which makes the power budget straightforward. Rotation is limited (about 90° with standard pulses and up to roughly 190° with wide pulses per ServoCity), so the hip range of motion must be checked against this. Ball bearing and a standard 24-tooth spline allow common horns and brackets to attach to the leg structure. Some retailers list the model as replaced by newer programmable servos and one distributor quotes a 3-week lead time, so stock must be confirmed before ordering.

  2. NEMA 17 bipolar stepper (17HS15-1704S) with DRV8825 stepper driver carrier

    • Motor: $3.76/each (sale price; list price $4.70)
    • 17HS15-1704S motor product page at StepperOnline
    • 17HS15-1704S full datasheet

    • Driver: TODO: $X.XX/each
    • DRV8825 driver carrier product page at Pololu
    • DRV8825 datasheet (Texas Instruments)
    Pros Cons The motor is very inexpensive ($3.76) and has a downloadable datasheet with rated current (1.7 A), winding resistance (2.3 Ω), and inductance (4.0 mH). The motor weighs 280 g, about six times the HS-485HB, for a similar holding torque (42 N·cm, about 4.3 kgf·cm), which adds mass to the shoulder assembly. The DRV8825 provides up to 1/32 microstepping from a 1.8° step motor, so position resolution is much finer than a hobby servo with no feedback sensor. The DRV8825 needs an 8.2–45 V motor supply, so it cannot run from the 5–6 V logic rail and adds a second power rail, regulator, and budget line. The Nano only has to output STEP and DIR pulses (plus optional ENABLE and nFAULT), with no PWM timing constraints. The motor's 1.7 A rating exceeds the carrier's roughly 1.5 A without a heat sink, so a heat sink or a lower current limit (and less torque) is needed. The shaft holds position while the coils are energized and there is no gear train to strip, and rotation is not limited to 90–190°. It is open loop: lost steps under overload go undetected, so the joint needs a homing switch at power-up. The DRV8825 has built-in over-current protection, thermal shutdown, undervoltage lockout, and an adjustable current limit. Torque falls with speed, the motor can resonate, and the coils draw current continuously while holding, which wastes power and creates heat. Two parts must be bought and wired (STEP, DIR, ENABLE, power, and four motor wires), and the current-limit potentiometer must be set before connecting the motor.

  3. SG92R micro servo

    • TODO: $X.XX/each
    • SG92R product page at ProtoSupplies
    Pros Cons At about 9 g and roughly 22 × 12 × 27 mm it adds almost no mass to the leg. Stall torque is quoted as 1.5 to 2.5 kgf·cm depending on the source, well below the 4.8–6.0 kgf·cm of the HS-485HB. Measured stall current is around 650 mA with 100–300 mA while moving, which is lower than the HS-485HB. Reseller specifications disagree with each other and there is no authoritative manufacturer datasheet, which conflicts with the course guidance on datasheets. It is inexpensive and uses the same one-pin PWM interface and Servo library as the HS-485HB. Plastic gears with no ball bearing wear quickly under load, and sustained stall can overheat the motor. It runs from the 5 V rail with no extra driver or supply. There is no position feedback, and the limited torque leaves little margin for a leg joint.

Choice: Option 1: Hitec HS-485HB standard servo

Rationale: The HS-485HB is the best match for the Driver Nano 1 architecture. Its internal closed-loop position control means the Nano only needs one PWM pin and the standard Servo library, and it runs from the same 4.8–6 V supply as the rest of the subsystem. The stepper option (Option 2) is the most inexpensive motor, but the DRV8825 needs at least 8.2 V, which forces a second power rail and regulator, and the 280 g motor is about six times heavier than the servo for similar torque. The SG92R (Option 3) is lightest, but its torque is too low and its datasheet values are unreliable. The HS-485HB's 6.0 kgf·cm at 6 V gives a margin over the required torque calculated above (TODO: state required torque and the resulting safety factor). Its 1.2 A stall current at 6 V is the main cost, and the power budget and regulator selection are sized for it with the 25% margin, with the servo on its own regulated rail and not the Nano's 5V pin.

Diagnostic Display (leg status)

  1. 0.96" 128×64 monochrome OLED module, SSD1306 controller (Amazon listing)

    • TODO: $X.XX/each (copy from the listing)
    • 0.96" SSD1306 OLED module on Amazon
    • TODO: add a link to the SSD1306 controller datasheet or the datasheet in the listing (required for Amazon parts).
    Pros Cons The I2C version needs only four wires (VCC, GND, SDA, SCL), which uses very few Nano pins. The listing must provide a datasheet or detailed specifications, and the module's board layout (pin order, on-board regulator) can vary between sellers, so the listing must be checked before wiring. The panel emits its own light, giving high contrast with no backlight, and current draw is tens of mA depending on how many pixels are lit. OLED pixels dim with age and burn in if the same content is shown for thousands of hours, so the screen should be turned off when idle. 128×64 pixels shows several lines of status (commanded angle, measured status, fault flags) or a simple graphic. The Adafruit_SSD1306 library keeps a 1 KB frame buffer, half of the Nano's 2 KB SRAM, so the U8g2 library in page-buffer mode (about 128 bytes) should be used instead. U8g2 supports software I2C on any two digital pins, so the display can avoid the hardware I2C pins (A4/A5) used for the command bus to the Main Nano. At 0.96" diagonal the text is small, which limits readability from a distance. It is the most inexpensive way to get a graphic display, and both U8g2 and Adafruit_SSD1306 are well documented. Software I2C is slower than hardware I2C, although this is not a problem for a status screen.

  2. Adafruit 0.96" 128×64 monochrome OLED, STEMMA QT (ADA326)

    • $17.50/each (quantity 1–9)
    • Adafruit 0.96" OLED (ADA326) product page
    • Adafruit monochrome OLED datasheets and design files
    Pros Cons Adafruit publishes datasheets, EagleCAD PCB files, and a full tutorial, which satisfies the course datasheet requirement without extra searching. It costs $17.50, which is more than a generic module with the same SSD1306 panel. The revised board has auto-reset circuitry, so the RESET pin is not needed, and I2C is the default configuration. The pins are not pre-soldered for breadboard use: it needs a STEMMA QT cable or soldered headers. The STEMMA QT connectors allow plug-in wiring without soldering. It has the same 1 KB frame-buffer cost as other SSD1306 modules when using the Adafruit library. Adafruit's library and tutorial are the reference implementation for the SSD1306. It is the same panel as Option 1, so it adds no display capability.

  3. Adafruit Standard 16×2 character LCD, HD44780, white on blue (ADA181)

    • TODO: $X.XX/each
    • Adafruit Standard LCD 16×2 (ADA181) product page
    Pros Cons Adafruit provides a datasheet with pin locations and the HD44780 command-set datasheet. It is text-only (16 characters × 2 rows), so it cannot show graphics or a compact status layout. The single-row 0.1" header suits breadboards and through-hole boards. It needs six Nano digital lines in 4-bit mode (versus two for an I2C OLED). Adding the I2C backpack would reduce the pins but add cost and put it on the I2C bus. The LiquidCrystal library ships with the Arduino IDE and uses very little RAM, so it avoids the OLED frame-buffer issue. A contrast potentiometer and backlight resistor are needed, and the backlight draws current continuously. The blue LED backlight can be dimmed with a resistor or PWM and uses much less power than EL backlights. The module is physically larger than the OLED.

Choice: Option 1: 0.96" 128×64 SSD1306 OLED module

Rationale: The OLED can show multiple lines of leg status (commanded angle, measured status, fault flags) and simple graphics, which the 16×2 LCD cannot. It needs only two signal pins, whereas the LCD needs six. Using the U8g2 library in page-buffer mode on software I2C (pins D4/D5) solves two Nano problems at once: it keeps only about 128 bytes of RAM in use, and it leaves the hardware I2C pins (A4/A5) free as the command bus to the Main Nano. The Adafruit module (Option 2) is the same panel at a higher price, so it is kept as the fallback if the Amazon listing does not provide a datasheet. TODO: confirm the Amazon listing includes a datasheet or detailed specifications.

Pin Table (draft, Driver Nano 1)

Nano pin Function Connects to D9 Servo signal (50 Hz PWM, Servo library) HS-485HB signal wire D4 OLED SDA (software I2C, U8g2) OLED SDA D5 OLED SCL (software I2C, U8g2) OLED SCL A4 Hardware I2C SDA (command/feedback bus) Main Processor Nano A5 Hardware I2C SCL (command/feedback bus) Main Processor Nano 5V / GND Logic power for the Nano and OLED Regulated 5 V rail (external) Servo power, 6 V rail, sized for 1.2 A stall HS-485HB power wire, common ground with the Nano

If the stepper option is chosen instead: D2 = STEP, D3 = DIR, D6 = ENABLE, D7 = nFAULT (input), with the motor supply (8.2 V or higher) on the DRV8825 VMOT pin.
